Author made good points about the goals of our educational system, and how misguided it is. However, I really don't think they made a good case for why it ought to be reverent of cultural traditions as an alternative, though as the ending of the article shows (see bold below), the author is clearly deeply committed to a lost heritage (for, again, unspecified reasons).

On our best days, I discern their longing and anguish and I know that their innate human desire to know who they are, where they have come from, where they ought to go, and how they ought to live will always reassert itself.

Cultural inheritance provides little here, our ancestors were astonishingly ignorant about who we are, where we came from, and where we ought to go. We can make far more clear-eyed judgments on each of these factors in light of modern, secular science and reason.

But even on those better days, I can’t help but hold the hopeful thought that the world they have inherited – a world without inheritance, without past, future, or deepest cares –

A world willing to move forward, and dispense with the prejudices and superstitions of the past is not without future, and far from without deepest cares--these things need not be tied to tradition, religion, or culture, but can be reasoned.

is about to come tumbling down, and that this collapse would be the true beginning of a real education.

This is the author's "hopeful thought"? Think about that.

I think you make excellent points, it need not be a wholly negative proposition. However, when you see the way students are becoming little tyrants, crying out for their baby blanket and for safe spaces, and for curtailing the freedom of speech and expression that are the grand historical traditions of academia, I think it becomes more clear why this is such a bad thing. I was an exceptional student, and I can tell you, from a very early age, the educational system failed me and its preference was in favor of the mass hive of worker drones they were trying to create. It took many years for me to come to terms with and resolve this, and I sympathize with the author because I can't help but wonder at the world we might create if we were able to, not only address the needs of the majority, but also had a way to cultivate those students with a higher capacity for learning. If we could do this, we might even be so bold as to tease out those students in the majority who are just on the cusp of being in this group that integrates knowledge at a faster rate. I dare to believe we surely couldn't be any worse off. I've known many people who were also exceptional students, and by far, the ones that were home schooled were far more well adjusted and free from having had to overcome the mental restraints that our educational system imposes. When I look at all of the great autodidacts, the core trait that they all share in common is that they were people with a passion for the subjects they immersed themselves in. As the author mentions, the students of today are geared towards gaming the system, passing the requisite tests, but not mastering or integrating any of actual information. I do understand why he is hopeful for it all to come tumbling down. Then we can start the work of rebuilding it. Hopefully it will be able to be remade, and free from the accretion of all of the misguided mistakes and social indoctrination of the past 50 or so years.
